analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal employment discrimination remedies and extends civil rights protections to congressional employees.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 46 House Republicans, never advanced past its subcommittee referrals and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without any hearing or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it easier for workers to prove race, sex, religion, or national origin discrimination, let courts order employers to pay up to $150,000 in extra damages, and extended employment discrimination protections to employees of the House, Senate, and congressional agencies. It also included safeguards for employers, such as a cap on damages and a rule that non-discriminatory drug policies are lawful. It was the Republican-led version of a civil rights bill, introduced the day after the House failed to override the President's veto of the Democratic version, and it never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers facing employment discrimination — including women, racial minorities, religious minorities, and older workers — would gain clearer legal standards, stronger remedies (up to $150,000 in additional damages plus attorney's and expert fees), a longer window to sue the federal government, and a restored right to sue over private contracts. Congressional employees, who are currently outside most federal employment discrimination laws, would gain coverage for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: Makes an employment practice unlawful when race, color, religion, sex, or national origin was a motivating factor, even if other factors also played a role — instead of requiring it to be the sole reason.

Lets courts order an employer found to have intentionally discriminated to pay up to $150,000 in additional money damages to the worker, when needed to deter discrimination and justified by the equities.

Defines the 'business necessity' defense in disparate-impact cases and lets workers win by proving an equally effective, comparable-cost alternative practice existed that the employer refused to adopt.

Restores the right to make and enforce contracts free of racial discrimination against private as well as government actors, covering the making, performance, modification, and termination of contracts and all their terms and benefits.
Extends the deadline for federal employees to sue over job discrimination from 30 to 90 days and gives them the same interest on delayed payments as private litigants.

Applies federal employment discrimination protections to employees of the House, Senate, congressional agencies, and instrumentalities like the Architect of the Capitol and GAO, which today fall largely outside those laws.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and labor organizations that lose discrimination cases would pay damages capped at $150,000, plus attorney's fees, expert fees, and interest. The federal government would owe interest to employees it made wait for relief. Members of Congress and congressional agencies would have to comply with the same anti-discrimination laws they apply to private employers.

drawbacks.text: Caps the additional damages award at $150,000 per case, a limit that can leave badly injured workers with less compensation than a court might otherwise order and that falls well short of the unlimited remedy sought in the rival Democratic bill.
Lets employers escape all monetary relief by proving they would have made the same decision even without discrimination — the worker could get only a declaration, an injunction, and fees.

Requires 'demonstrable evidence' for the business-necessity defense and spells out a specific standard, which in practice could make it harder for workers to win disparate-impact cases against facially neutral practices like tests or experience requirements.

Bars employees and applicants who had notice from challenging court-approved or consent judgments settling discrimination cases, limiting their ability to contest settlement terms they were never party to.
Leaves most issues to be decided by a judge rather than a jury, with juries only for liability on the capped damages claims if a court finds the Constitution requires it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have net strengthened protections for discrimination victims — clearer proof standards, real money damages, longer filing windows, and coverage of congressional employment — while deliberately limiting employer exposure with a $150,000 cap, a same-decision defense, and an explicit no-quotas provision. An honest supporter would call it a middle-ground package: less relief for workers than the Democratic bill that was vetoed, but real relief nonetheless, and the congressional-employee coverage would have ended a carve-out from the law's own enforcers. Even that modest package never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees, and never came up again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: House Minority Leader Robert Michel introduced the bill on October 23, 1990, with 45 other original cosponsors, all Republicans.
It was referred the same day to four committees — Education and Labor, Judiciary, House Administration, and Rules.
The House Personnel and Police Subcommittee received it on October 27 and the Civil and Constitutional Rights Subcommittee on November 16; no hearing or further action followed.
The bill sat without any floor action and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, labor organizations, and the federal government were better off because the bill died — they kept the existing, narrower remedies for discrimination victims. Congressional offices also avoided being covered by the employment discrimination laws they apply to private employers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers kept the narrower status quo

for.name: Robert H. Michel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as the lead sponsor

against.name: House Democratic majority
against.role: Controlled committee calendars and the floor agenda
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referring it to four committees and two subcommittees; no hearing was ever held and no vote was ever scheduled

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Had just vetoed the stronger Democratic Civil Rights Act of 1990 the day before this bill was introduced, and the House failed to override, keeping the broader bill from law

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 46 in all — was a House Republican, and the Democratic majority never moved the bill; it was the Republican response to a Democratic civil rights bill that had already passed both chambers and been vetoed.

industries.note: The bill would have created new liability for hiring, promotion, and firing practices with discriminatory effects, with awards up to $150,000 plus fees. It also gave employers protections they sought — a drug-policy carve-out, an explicit business-necessity standard, and a same-decision defense — so the hit was deliberately moderate.

industries.industry: Congress as an employer (members and congressional agencies)
industries.note: For the first time, Senate, House, and congressional-agency employees would have been covered by the same federal anti-discrimination laws applied to everyone else, with claims handled inside each chamber's own procedures. Today those workplaces largely exempt themselves.
Unions and joint labor-management apprenticeship programs count as 'respondents' and would face the same expanded remedies and standards as employers in discrimination cases.
